en: What's very important to understand when
working with large language models is that
the large language model itself is really
just text in, text out, or specifically
tokens in, tokens out. It has no brain, it
has no memory, it has no internal database,
none of that.
It can replicate a thinking process by
simply,
well,
chaining token after token and describing a
thought process just as if you think. It's
just in the end a sequence of text, right?
So a model can do that. That too.
But it still has no brain, it still has no
way of, for example, writing files on your
system or anything like that.
If you want a tool that can do more and that
uses a large language model as its brain,
that uses this replicated thought process in
the end to make decisions,
you need to build a so-called AI agent, you
need to build a system, a software that
wraps such a large language model, that
communicates to such a large language model,
and that then acts on behalf of the large
language model. And that's what's typically
referred to as an AI agent nowadays. But
even ChatGPT, the website or the desktop
application you can install,
even that is in the end such an AI agent.
Because even that in the end sits between
you and your input and the output that was
produced by an underlying large language
model.
And if you, for example, attach a PDF
document to ChatGPT, that document gets
opened and parsed by the ChatGPT tool,
and the text inside of that document is then
submitted along with your prompt to the
large language model running somewhere on
the OpenAI servers. That's how you have to
think about that. It's always software plus
the underlying large language model.
And if we're building even smarter AI agents
that can, for example, search your file
system or generate files or read files and
edit files, then what we're in the end
building is AI agents that expose tools to
AI models, to large language models, and let
those models decide which tool to use in
which situation. But we'll take a look at
that in a separate lecture.
